name: Pine pollen (Songhwa)

card.summary: Powdered pine pollen taken as a tonic in Korean and Chinese tradition, used by some people hoping for better energy, skin and hormone support.
card.note: Pine pollen can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive people; claims about hormones rest mostly on lab and animal work.

quick.overview:
Pine pollen, known in Korea as songhwa garu, is the fine yellow powder shed by pine trees. It is traditionally eaten in Korea as an ingredient in sweets and beverages, and in Traditional Chinese Medicine it has been used as a tonic for fatigue and aging.

In appearance and fitness circles it is taken as a plant-based supplement with claimed support for testosterone, energy, recovery and a younger look. Published work consists mostly of cell, animal and compositional studies.
quick.how: It is sold as a powder or capsule and stirred into drinks or foods, often as a daily supplement. Proponents describe it as a long-term tonic rather than something with quick results.
quick.risks: Inhaled pine pollen can cause allergic rhinitis, conjunctivitis and asthma flares, with sensitization reported in roughly 2 to 12 percent of tested allergic people. Safety of ingested supplements has not been well studied, and the FDA does not allow bee-pollen marketers to make health claims.

lead: Pine pollen is the powdery male reproductive material of pine trees, with winged grains suited to wind dispersal [1]. In Korea, where it is called songhwa garu, it is traditionally consumed in sweets and beverages [1]. In Traditional Chinese Medicine it has been used to tonify qi, nourish the kidneys and support longevity [2].

People interested in appearance take it as a general vitality tonic. Proponents claim support for testosterone, energy, libido, muscle recovery and antioxidant and anti-aging effects, which they connect to better skin, training and physique [2]. Reported composition includes protein, carbohydrates, lipids, polyphenols and minerals, plus trace plant-derived androgens such as testosterone and androstenedione reported in Scots pine [2].

Research on pine pollen is mostly laboratory and animal work. A 2012 study found pine pollen delayed senescence in human fibroblast cells and in a mouse aging model [3], and a 2009 paper reported antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in vitro [4].

paras: Pine pollen grains are winged, which helps them travel on wind [1]. Protein reportedly makes up about 11 to 51 percent depending on species and environment, with carbohydrates, lipids, polyphenols and minerals such as magnesium, calcium and iron [2].

Korean tradition uses songhwa garu as an ingredient in sweets and drinks [1]. Chinese tradition uses pine pollen as a tonic for fatigue, immunity and aging [2]. Modern marketers also position it as an adaptogenic supplement for hormones, libido and recovery [2].

Proponents point to reported phytoandrogens, including brassinosteroids and trace androgens in Scots pine, as a reason it may support testosterone [2]. Reviews note that evidence is mostly in vitro, animal or small observational work, and that rigorous human trials are lacking [2].

Inhaled pine pollen can cause allergic rhinitis, conjunctivitis and asthma flares, with sensitization of about 2 to 12 percent among tested allergic people, and some symptoms may come from mechanical irritation [2]. In a 1988 clinical study in New England, 6 of 100 consecutive allergic-rhinitis patients had a positive skin test to eastern white pine pollen [5].

No human trials of ingested pine pollen for appearance or hormones were found. Related laboratory work includes a 2012 study of pine pollen in human fibroblasts and D-galactose-aged mice [3], a 2009 in vitro antioxidant study [4], and a 2016 study of sulfated pine pollen polysaccharides on mouse macrophages [6]. A 1988 allergy study assessed sensitivity, not benefit [5].
